title: Research
text:
With Juan Durán Vanegas and Iulia Siedschlag. ESRI Working Paper No. 812, October 2025.
[Paper] [Policy brief]
This paper examines the role of human capital in driving labour-productivity growth across industries in the European Union and the United Kingdom from 2010 to 2021. Building on Égert et al. (2022), we introduce an industry-level quality-adjusted human capital (QAHC) measure that combines the quantity of education with its quality, drawing on test-score data from the OECD Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) and Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC), mean years of schooling, and industry employment composition from EU KLEMS and INTANProd. Estimated within a Stochastic Frontier framework, the measure yields plausible output elasticities and is statistically associated with labour-productivity growth, particularly in goods-producing industries. These results stand in contrast to those obtained using conventional education-attainment proxies, which fail to capture a comparable productivity link.

title: Research
text:
Theses

Behavioural Responses to Targeted Housing Subsidies: Evidence from Ireland’s Help to Buy Scheme
MRes thesis, Sciences Po, May 2026. Supervisor: Antoine Ferey.
This thesis studies how a targeted housing subsidy affects behaviour at an eligibility cut-off and participation within the subsidised market. I examine Ireland’s Help to Buy scheme, which subsidises first-time buyers of new-build dwellings valued at or below €500,000. Using property sales and household purchase records, I combine a model of developers’ responses with bunching and difference-in-differences designs. I find excess mass just below €500,000 in the new-build market, but not before the policy or among second-hand transactions, alongside a substantial shift of first-time buyers towards new-builds. When the scheme became more generous in 2020, bunching increased by 55%, closely matching the 50% increase in the maximum relief available at the cut-off. The reallocation of first-time buyers towards new-builds roughly doubled, in line with the doubling of the headline subsidy rate. Each margin therefore responds almost proportionally to a different dimension of policy generosity. The threshold and participation margins are linked through the eligible share of demand in the new-build market. Under universal coverage, all demand is exposed to losing eligibility at the cut-off; under targeted coverage, only the eligible share is exposed, and that share varies with buyer participation. More generous subsidies therefore strengthen the threshold response through both the value of eligibility and the share of demand exposed.


The Impact of Light Rail Transit Extensions on Residential Property Prices: Evidence from Dublin’s Luas Cross City Project
Undergraduate thesis, Trinity College Dublin, April 2024. Supervisor: Ronan Lyons.
[Thesis]
This dissertation investigates the capitalisation of light rail transit (LRT) access into residential property prices, using the 2017 Luas Cross City extension in Dublin as a quasi-experimental setting. I estimate the treatment effect using hedonic pricing, difference-in-differences, and instrumental-variables designs, identifying the response of prices to distance from new stops. To mitigate endogeneity in route and station placement, I instrument for proximity to the extension with distance to Dublin’s nineteenth-century historical rail network. The analysis documents a non-linear distance gradient: the DiD specification yields a 5.78% post-opening price premium within 1,000 metres of a new stop, whilst the IV specification estimates a 13.1% premium in the 400–800 metre band. The findings are consistent with the view that anticipated and realised transport-accessibility gains are internalised into the local housing market, and contribute to the growing quasi-experimental literature on light rail and land values.

title: Michelle Alicia Jordan
text:
I am an applied microeconomist. My research is in public and urban economics, with a particular interest in policies whose effects are heterogeneous across space or along the income and wealth distribution. Topics I work on include housing and transport policy, behavioural distortions from tax-benefit instruments, and the interaction between public interventions and local markets.
I am currently completing an MRes in Economics at Sciences Po, Paris, following a B.A. (Hons.) in Economics and Social Studies at Trinity College Dublin. I am delighted to be moving to London in the autumn of 2026 to join CenTax as a Research Economist.
